title: Accuracy-First Rényi Differential Privacy and Post-Processing Immunity
claim: Our bound matches the best tuned prior bounds, and prior bounds degrade when tuned for only one parameter value.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared y-axis, log scale, legends inside
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a log-scale y-axis (Sigma, 10^0 to 10^2) and an x-axis for Epsilon (ADP, delta = 10^-5), running from 0 to 10. Each panel has a grid and a legend in the upper right. The left panel is titled 'Mixture & Linear Tuned Per-sigma'. A solid blue curve for the RDP bound (Ours) falls steeply and then flattens. The dotted orange optimised-linear and dashed green optimised-mixture curves almost overlap it. The right panel is titled 'Mixture & Linear Tuned for One sigma'. The blue RDP curve stays at the bottom. Linear and mixture bounds tuned at sigma=1 or sigma=10 (orange, green, red and purple, dotted or dashed) drift above it. The linear bound at sigma=1 shoots up vertically near epsilon 2.4. The eye goes first to the blue curve, then to the diverging colored curves in the right panel.
caption: Comparison of our ex-post RDP-based bound and the bounds of [ref] (mixture and linear) for the Brownian mechanism in approximate-ex-post privacy ([ref]), showing all bounds are very similar. This is assuming probabilistic ex-post privacy implies approximate ex-post privacy, which we conjecture is true since it is true in ex-ante DP. In the left panel, we optimise all free parameters of each bound individually for each value of $\sigma$. In the right panel, we use the recommended procedure of [ref] for their bounds, meaning we optimise them for a specific $\sigma$, either 1 or 10. This makes these bounds suboptimal for other values of $\sigma$.
abstract: The accuracy-first perspective of differential privacy addresses an important shortcoming by allowing a data analyst to adaptively adjust the quantitative privacy bound instead of sticking to a predetermined bound. Existing works on the accuracy-first perspective have neglected an important property of differential privacy known as post-processing immunity, which ensures that an adversary is not able to weaken the privacy guarantee by post-processing. We address this gap by determining which existing definitions in the accuracy-first perspective have post-processing immunity, and which do not. The only definition with post-processing immunity, pure ex-post privacy, lacks useful tools for practical problems, such as an ex-post analogue of the Gaussian mechanism, and an algorithm to check if accuracy on separate private validation set is high enough. To address this, we propose a new definition based on RÃ©nyi differential privacy that has post-processing immunity, and we develop basic theory and tools needed for practical applications. We demonstrate the practicality of our theory with applications to synthetic data generation and image classifier fine-tuning, where our algorithm successfully adjusts the privacy bound until an accuracy threshold is met on a private validation dataset.
